D018-D020_h001.question: I’ve been having these nightmares almost every other night since it happened—same dream, mostly. I’m back at the gas station during the robbery, hearing the gunshots, seeing my coworker fall. I wake up sweating, heart racing, and it takes forever to calm down. Sometimes I’m shaky for like, half an hour. It’s been four months now, and I just can’t get back to normal. I don’t even want to go to work most days. The shift manager said I’ve been slacking, but I can’t force myself to care like I used to. I keep thinking it shouldn’t have gone down like that… if only Marcus hadn’t argued with the guy, maybe none of it would’ve happened. I know it sounds harsh, but he made it worse. I feel bad saying that, but I can’t shake the shame either—like I should’ve done something more. Even small things mess me up now. D018-D020_h002.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since the car accident seven months ago. I still see it over and over—especially at night. I keep having these dreams where I’m stuck in the car, glass everywhere, and I can’t move. When I wake up, my heart’s racing like I’m still there. Even during the day, I can’t relax. I flinch every time a car door slams or someone honks—my body just jerks, and my husband says I look terrified.

I used to love meeting friends for coffee, but now I cancel plans last minute. It’s not that I don’t want to see them… I just feel numb, like I’m disconnected from everything. I blame myself constantly—why did I insist on driving that night? I could’ve taken an Uber. The guilt eats at me.

Even small decisions overwhelm me. I’ll stand in front of the closet for twenty minutes trying to pick an outfit. At work, I can’t focus—clicking “submit” on a design feels impossible. I’ve been like this since the accident, and it hasn’t gotten better. If anything, it’s worse. I used to be confident; now I feel like I’m always on edge, waiting for something else to go wrong.
D018-D020_h002.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h003.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since the accident last year—when the commuter train I was on derailed. It’s been over six months, but I can’t seem to move past it. I still get this tightness in my chest and shaky hands whenever I see a train or even hear a loud horn—sometimes just thinking about it sends my heart racing. I don’t feel like myself anymore. I used to love cooking with my husband, laughing over burnt dinners, but now I don’t get any joy from things I once loved. I feel numb most days.

I keep replaying the crash. I survived, but others didn’t, and I can’t shake the guilt—like I should’ve done something, or that I didn’t deserve to make it. I even find myself angry at the transit authority, at the engineers—anyone but myself, maybe. It’s easier to blame them than sit with how helpless I felt.

Making even small choices feels impossible now. What to wear, what to eat—I stall for ages, second-guessing everything. And if someone walks into the room suddenly, I flinch hard, like I’m back there. It’s been months, but these symptoms haven’t let up—they’re constant.
D018-D020_h003.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h004.question: I keep seeing it over and over—the noise, the blood, people screaming. D018-D020_h005.question: I’ve been struggling since the school shooting last year—a student brought a gun onto campus.     D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h006.question:
I’ve been struggling since that tractor accident last year—my son was nearly crushed, and I couldn’t get to him fast enough. Even now, out of nowhere, I’ll see it all again—the blood, the sound—like I’m right back there. It happens when I’m feeding the animals or even just sitting at the table. I try not to think about it, but the harder I push it away, the more it seems to come back uninvited. Sometimes I can’t even talk about it with my wife; I shut down, feel hollow, like there’s no room inside for anything—good or bad. I don’t laugh like I used to, not even with the grandkids.

I remember pieces of the accident—the noise of the engine, pulling him out—but whole chunks are just gone, and that bothers me. The worst part is how I’ve been snapping lately. Last week, I yelled at a neighbor for parking too close to the gate—over nothing. And if someone touches my shoulder from behind, I jump hard, sometimes even swing out without thinking. These symptoms haven’t gone away. It’s been over a year now, and they’re still with me, every day, making it harder to work, to be with my family.
D018-D020_h006.options:

    C. Binge-Eating Disorder

D018-D020_h007.question:

I keep reliving it out of nowhere: sitting at my desk, and suddenly I’m back there, heart pounding, tasting blood from when I bit my tongue. I remember the knife, the voice, but everything right after I fell—total blank. I’ve blocked out parts, but not all, which terrifies me.

I avoid that whole stretch of street now; won’t even ride the subway at night. I used to love going out with friends, but I cancel plans constantly. Even my sister calls, and I don’t answer—something in me just shuts down. I know I care about her, but I can’t *feel* it, not like before. I used to fall easily in love—now I feel nothing, even when someone’s kind to me.

And the anger—I didn’t used to be like this. Last week I screamed at a coworker over a typo. My producer pulled me aside. And if someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly? I jump out of my skin, literally yell at them. It’s been months, and it’s not getting better. If anything, it’s like my body’s stuck in emergency mode.
D018-D020_h007.options:

    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Binge-Eating Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h008.question:

What scares me most is how empty I feel. My sister says I’ve changed—I don’t hug her anymore, and when my ex reached out, I couldn’t bring myself to care, even though I used to love him. It’s been over a year, and I’m not getting better. Some days, I feel like I’m just surviving, not living.

D018-D020_h009.question:

I used to love teaching—the joy of it, seeing people relax. But now, even when a student tells me I helped them, I don’t feel anything. D018-D020_h010.question:

Before all this, I loved cooking—I used to beam when my sauces turned out right. Now, even if my chef instructor praises me, it just… doesn’t feel like anything. D018-D020_h011.question:

I keep seeing his face, the child screaming… it floods back during quiet moments, even in staff meetings. I’ll start shaking, my chest tightens—it’s like I’m back there. I avoid case notes on similar cases, skip supervision if the topic comes up. Honestly, I don’t open my work email after hours.  

I feel… ruined. Like I can’t trust myself anymore. Before, I believed I could help these families, but now I think I’m just making things worse. Maybe I *am* reckless—like I deserved what almost happened. My husband says it wasn’t my fault, but I can’t stop thinking: if I had handled it differently, it wouldn’t have come to that. Sometimes I snap at him—yell, curse—over nothing. He walks on eggshells, and I hate that, but I can’t seem to stop the anger before it bursts.  

It’s been six months, and I thought I’d feel better by now. But it’s not fading—it’s getting harder to pretend I’m okay.

D018-D020_h012.question:

They knew the warnings. They minimized the threats. I wouldn’t be like this if they hadn’t been so reckless.  

I snap at people—my secretary, my daughter, strangers on the phone. My ex-wife says I’ve become “impossible.” Truth is, I’m tired of feeling like I’m always under threat, even in my own apartment. I thought it’d pass after a few weeks, but it’s only gotten worse. This isn’t just stress—it’s like my whole mind’s stuck there, reliving it, guarding against it, angry it ever happened.
D018-D020_h012.options:

D018-D020_h013.question:

I don’t talk about it—not with my wife, not with anyone. I can’t stand thinking about it, so I push it away. I stay busy with forecasts, work longer hours. But when I do zone out, I go dark—thinking I’m a liability, that I should’ve seen it coming, that I’m broken somehow. I blame the incident commander who sent us in—he ignored the shifting data. I yelled at my wife last month for no reason—just snapped when she asked about it. I’ve always been calm, but now I’m on edge, like the storm’s still coming. I thought I’d get past it, but it only feels worse.

D018-D020_h014.question: I’ve been struggling since the car accident last year—my driver was killed when our vehicle was attacked during a conflict zone visit for work. It’s not like me. I’ve tried to pull myself together, but it’s been months now, and if anything, it’s getting worse. I thought I’d bounce back—doctors aren’t supposed to fall apart—but I can’t seem to turn it off.
